title: Start From a Template, or a Blank Prompt?
metaDescription: Kodely's templates are starter prompts, not layouts. What that changes about how you begin, and when a blank box is the better start.
body: Every website builder has templates. On most of them a template is a finished layout you pour your content into, and the whole job is bending your business to fit someone else's structure.

Kodely's templates are not that. They are prompts — the text lands in the composer, you edit it, and the site gets generated from your version. Which means choosing between "template" and "blank prompt" is a much smaller decision than it sounds, and a genuinely useful one to understand.
What a template actually is here

Pick a template and what you get is a full starter brief in the prompt box: the audience, the purpose, the tone, the sections, and bracketed placeholders where only you know the facts — [your opening hours], [your price], [link to your booking system].

Nothing is generated until you press build. So the template is not a layout you are stuck inside; it is a well-written first message you are free to gut. Delete half of it, change the tone line, add three sections it did not think of. The result is still a site generated from a description — yours.

The gallery covers the verticals a one-page site actually suits: food and drink, beauty and wellness, local services, professional services, personal and creative, startup and product, events and causes.
Why the templates are written the way they are
The interesting constraint is what the starter prompts deliberately never ask for.

None of them asks for a working contact or booking form, an account, a cart, a database or an API call. None asks for a remote image, a custom web font, or a second page either. Not because those would look bad, but because a generated site genuinely cannot do them — the full list is here — and a starter prompt that asked for one would be a trap set by the product itself.

Where a vertical normally leans on something impossible — bookings, RSVPs, donations, checkout, waitlists — the prompt asks for a link-out instead: a mailto:, a tel:, or a clearly bracketed link to the tool you already use. And the card describing the template says so in plain language, so nobody picks "Restaurant" expecting a reservation system.
That is worth checking on any builder you evaluate: whether its templates promise things its engine cannot deliver.
When to start from a template

• You are not sure what sections the page needs. The starter prompt is a checklist written by someone who has thought about this vertical.
  • You freeze at an empty box. Editing beats composing, and this converts the job into editing.
  • You want to see how a good prompt is written. Read one closely — the structure of it is the actual lesson, and it transfers to every prompt you write afterwards.
  • Your business is close to a standard shape. A barber, a coffee shop, a consultant. The starter is 80% right before you touch it.
When to start blank

• You have a strong visual idea. A template prompt carries tone and palette suggestions you will end up arguing with. Faster to state yours.
  • Your business is genuinely odd. Two businesses in one room, an unusual service model, a page with one strange job to do. A generic starter drags you towards the average.
  • You already know the sections. Then the template is a longer route to the same place.

And there is a middle path most people end up on: start blank with one line, press Enhance, and get a full brief generated from your own idea rather than a category. Enhance is free and is not recorded as a build — a preview of what you are about to spend on should not itself cost anything.
Either way, edit before you build
This is the part that matters more than the choice. Whatever lands in the box, read it and replace every bracket you can before pressing build.

Left in, a bracket stays on the page as a bracket. That is the intended behaviour — the builder writes [your phone number] rather than inventing one, because an invented phone number is a real stranger's phone number. But it does mean a first build from an unedited template is a scaffold, not a site.
Spending four minutes filling in brackets before the first build is the highest-value four minutes in the whole process, and it saves a round of edits afterwards.
The short version

1. A template here is a starter prompt, not a layout. Nothing about it is locked.
  2. They are written to stay inside what a generated site can genuinely do, and to link out where it cannot.
  3. Start from one when you want a checklist; start blank when you have a strong idea.
  4. Fill in the brackets before the first build, either way.
